---
name: interface-forge-mobile
description: Design, build, redesign, and validate production mobile interfaces for responsive mobile web, PWAs, iOS, Android, React Native, Flutter, and mobile companion experiences. Use for onboarding, authentication, mobile dashboards and widgets, navigation, gestures, forms, timers, activity tracking, media, chat, file management, commerce, settings, offline behavior, safe areas, software keyboards, light/dark/OLED themes, accessibility, or mobile UI quality assurance. Do not use for desktop-first dashboards, landing pages, or browser-extension surfaces; use the corresponding Interface Forge specialist.
---

# Interface Forge Mobile

Build touch-first mobile products that respect platform behavior, constrained attention, variable connectivity, safe areas, text scaling and one-handed use. Preserve the existing framework and native conventions.

## Operating contract

1. Identify whether the target is mobile web/PWA, iOS, Android, React Native, Flutter or a companion surface; do not pretend their components and lifecycle are identical.
2. Inspect current navigation, design tokens, state/data architecture, platform minimums and available device/preview tools.
3. Design complete task flows, not disconnected screens. Include entry, progress, recovery, interruption and completion.
4. Keep primary actions reachable, labels specific and state durable across backgrounding, navigation, network loss and process restoration where the platform supports it.
5. Verify on representative small/large devices, text scaling, orientation, keyboard, reduced motion, light/dark mode and offline/error states.

## Phase 0 — Route the platform

Read [platform adaptation](references/platform-adaptation.md). Establish target platforms, minimum OS/browser versions, input methods, device classes, offline expectation, permissions, notification behavior and delivery format.

Read [tool routing](references/tool-routing.md) when simulators, screenshots, media tools or deployment capabilities vary. Reuse platform-native navigation, controls and accessibility APIs unless a custom implementation has a clear product reason.

## Phase 1 — Define the flow

Record the user goal, entry points, primary task, expected session length, interruption/recovery behavior, identity/auth state, permissions, local/remote data ownership, monetization and privacy constraints.

Map:

- screen and modal/sheet hierarchy;
- persistent versus ephemeral state;
- loading, empty, error, offline, stale, denied and completion states;
- deep links, notifications and back behavior;
- keyboard, gesture and assistive-technology paths.

## Phase 2 — Establish design grammar and themes

Read [style recipes](references/style-recipes.md) and select one coherent direction. Read [style packs](references/style-packs.md) when the brief calls for expressive reference-derived directions (aurora focus, neon arena, graphite glass, pastel glass, vivid tiles, playful gradient); apply their brand primitives from `assets/theme-packs.css` via `data-brand` without touching semantic roles. When the brief names a product idea, open [product blueprints](references/product-blueprints.md) first — `assets/blueprints.json` seeds recipe, pack, components, data grammar and first states for fifty common products, and its derivation procedure covers every other idea. Adapt its density, geometry and motion to the platform rather than shrinking a desktop composition.

Read [theme system](references/theme-system.md). Implement light and dark themes and add OLED only when useful. Respect system preference and explicit choice, safe-area surfaces, native control theming, dynamic type/font scaling, forced colors where applicable and contrast under real device brightness.

Use the shared assets in `assets/` as platform-neutral references. Use `assets/mobile-shell.css` for mobile web/PWA and `assets/native-token-map.json` to translate semantic roles to SwiftUI/UIKit, Compose/Views, React Native or Flutter.

## Phase 3 — Compose from mobile contracts

Read [component contracts](references/component-contracts.md), then inspect `assets/component-contracts.json`. For glow, gradient, glass, ring, tile and loader elements, read [advanced elements](references/advanced-elements.md) and compose from `assets/advanced-ui.css`; adapt community elements (uiverse and similar) only through its hardening checklist. Optional interactive polish (spotlight, tilt, count-up, tab keyboarding, toasts, dialogs with focus return, carousel dots, compare sliders, copy buttons, ticker pause) comes from `assets/ifx-behaviors.js` and must degrade cleanly when absent. When the brief asks for scrolling effects, 3D product motion, exploded views or cinematic story pages, read [3D product scrollytelling](references/scrollytelling-3d.md) — its section 0 adapts the contract to this surface — pick one recipe from `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` and drive it with `assets/scroll-scene.js`. Every selected element must satisfy its purpose, minimum visual/hit size, data requirements, interactions, accessibility, theme behavior, responsive adaptation and states.

Read [mobile layout and navigation](references/mobile-layout-navigation.md) for stack, tabs, drawers, rail/tablet and foldable behavior. Read [mobile input and gestures](references/mobile-input-gestures.md) for keyboard, focus, forms, gestures and permissions. Read [mobile data and widgets](references/mobile-data-widgets.md) for compact telemetry, charts and home-screen/widget-like cards.

## Phase 4 — Implement resilient behavior

- Keep coarse-pointer targets at least 44×44 CSS px/pt; use at least 48dp for Android touch targets unless a platform component provides equivalent accessible hit slop.
- Persist drafts and critical state before backgrounding or leaving a volatile surface.
- Make Back, Escape, dismissal, deep links and notification entry deterministic.
- Keep the focused field and primary action visible when the software keyboard opens.
- Provide explicit permission primer, denied and revoked flows; never block unrelated functionality.
- Design offline/read-only and sync-conflict behavior when the task can outlive a request.
- Use logical properties and direction-aware icons for RTL.
- Localize dates, units, currency and pluralization; test long translated content.

## Phase 5 — Motion, haptics and media

Read [mobile motion and haptics](references/mobile-motion-haptics.md). Use motion for continuity and feedback, not navigation delay. Haptics must reinforce a visible/audible outcome and respect platform/user settings. Avoid gesture-only actions and provide reduced-motion equivalents.

Media must reserve dimensions, adapt to bandwidth and data-saver preferences, expose playback controls and never autoplay audio.

## Phase 6 — Verify

Read [visual QA](references/visual-qa.md). Verify:

- smallest and largest supported phone classes plus one tablet/foldable layout when relevant;
- portrait and a meaningful landscape case;
- 200% browser zoom or maximum supported text scaling;
- safe areas, keyboard, Back/Escape, gestures and focus order;
- light, dark, OLED/high-contrast and reduced-motion behavior;
- offline, reconnect, stale, denied, empty, loading, error and restored-session states;
- primary flows with touch, keyboard and screen-reader semantics where tools permit;
- startup, list/scroll and media performance.

## Delivery standard

Report platforms, devices/viewports, flows and checks actually exercised. Identify platform-specific limitations rather than claiming false parity.

## Reference map

| Need | Read |
|---|---|
| Platform and framework adaptation | `references/platform-adaptation.md` |
| Navigation, layout, tablet and foldables | `references/mobile-layout-navigation.md` |
| Keyboard, forms, gestures and permissions | `references/mobile-input-gestures.md` |
| Compact data, telemetry and widgets | `references/mobile-data-widgets.md` |
| Motion and haptics | `references/mobile-motion-haptics.md` |
| Element behavior contracts | `references/component-contracts.md` + `assets/component-contracts.json` |
| Visual direction and themes | `references/style-recipes.md`, `references/theme-system.md` |
| Reference-derived packs and brand primitives | `references/style-packs.md` + `assets/theme-packs.css` |
| Expressive elements (glow, glass, rings, tiles) | `references/advanced-elements.md` + `assets/advanced-ui.css` |
| Blueprint for any product idea | `references/product-blueprints.md` + `assets/blueprints.json` |
| 3D product scrollytelling and exploded views | `references/scrollytelling-3d.md` + `references/scrollytelling-references.md` + `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` + `assets/scroll-scene.js` |
| QA | `references/visual-qa.md` |

# Mobile layout and navigation

## Navigation selection

| Structure | Use when | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Stack | Tasks have a clear drill-down path | Back preserves state and scroll; titles identify context |
| Bottom tabs | Three to five peer destinations are repeatedly used | Persistent labels; no transient action as a tab |
| Top tabs/segmented view | Peer views share one parent and limited labels | Correct tab semantics; controlled overflow |
| Drawer | Many lower-frequency destinations or account areas | Visible trigger, focus management, Back/Escape dismissal |
| Navigation rail | Tablet/foldable expanded widths | Same destinations and state as compact navigation |
| Sheet | Short contextual choice or task | Clear modality, drag handle plus explicit dismissal control |

Keep one source of navigation truth. Deep links and notification entry must produce the same state as in-app navigation.

## Layout rules

- Use a 4-column phone grid, 8-column medium grid and 12-column expanded grid only as alignment aids, not rigid templates.
- Keep primary content within reachable visual hierarchy; do not place every action at the bottom if keyboard or gesture bars obscure it.
- Use safe-area insets for edge-to-edge surfaces and floating actions.
- Allow text to wrap and vertical space to grow under scaling.
- Convert dense dashboard grids to prioritized vertical sequences, horizontally paged peer cards only when the continuation is obvious, or drill-down summaries.
- On tablets/foldables, use list-detail or supporting panes when both regions stay useful; avoid merely centering a narrow phone column.

## Back and dismissal

- Back navigates history, closes the top transient surface, or exits selection/edit mode in a documented order.
- Escape mirrors Back on keyboard-capable surfaces where appropriate.
- Destructive dismissal requires confirmation only when unsaved work would be lost.
- Gestural dismissal always has a visible, keyboard-accessible alternative.

# Mobile input and gestures

## Forms and software keyboard

- Use persistent labels, appropriate input types, autocomplete and platform autofill.
- Scroll the focused control and its error into view without obscuring it behind keyboard or sticky chrome.
- Keep submit available but prevent duplicate requests; preserve values on recoverable failure.
- Use field-level validation after meaningful interaction and a summary when multiple errors block submission.
- Never change user input formatting in a way that moves the cursor unpredictably.

## Gestures

- Treat tap as the primary universal gesture.
- Provide visible alternatives for swipe, drag, pinch and long press.
- Keep system edge, scrolling and text-selection gestures unblocked.
- Require confirmation or undo for destructive swipe actions.
- Give drag handles accessible names and keyboard/programmatic reorder alternatives.

## Permissions

1. Explain the user benefit immediately before a permission is needed.
2. Request only from an intentional user action.
3. Continue with reduced functionality when declined whenever possible.
4. Detect and explain denied and revoked states.
5. Link to system settings only when the user chooses to resolve the denial.

## Input diversity

Support touch plus keyboard/pointer on tablets, foldables and desktop-class mobile modes. Hover may enhance but never reveal the only action or meaning.

# Mobile data and widgets

Compact data components must remain informative rather than decorative.

## Telemetry grammar

Every metric widget includes value, unit, timeframe, freshness and threshold/target meaning when shown. Express trend and status in text as well as color or geometry.

| Pattern | Best use | Mobile adaptation |
|---|---|---|
| KPI card | One critical value and comparison | One headline; remove micro-chart before context |
| Sparkline | Supporting trend | At least 96×32 visual plus textual direction |
| Progress/ring | Known goal or completion | Exact value in center/adjacent; no angle-only meaning |
| Gauge | Bounded physical/operational range | Replace with bullet meter in narrow widgets |
| Calendar heatmap | Habit/frequency pattern | Show a shorter period or weekly summary |
| Line/area chart | Time trend | Fewer ticks, focusable points only when needed, alternate table/summary |
| Bar chart | Category comparison | Prefer horizontal bars for long labels |

## Widget-like surfaces

- Design glanceable states with one primary metric or action.
- Assume limited update frequency and stale data; show last updated when consequential.
- Do not require scrolling or hover.
- Ensure tap target opens a meaningful destination rather than an unrelated home screen.
- Test light/dark wallpapers or host surfaces when the platform allows translucent widgets.

## Dense dashboards

Prioritize three to seven questions, then build a vertical decision path. Use horizontal carousels only for truly peer cards and expose continuation. Move exact tables and complex filters to dedicated routes or sheets.

# Mobile motion and haptics

Use motion to preserve spatial continuity, confirm state and explain direct manipulation.

- Keep control feedback near-instant and route transitions brief.
- Preserve interruptibility; users can reverse navigation or dismiss without waiting.
- Disable parallax, looping ambience, autoplay and large spatial movement under reduced motion.
- Avoid animating layout continuously; use transforms and opacity when possible.
- Pause media/animation when backgrounded or offscreen.
- Use skeletons only when final geometry is predictable.

Use haptics for confirmed selection, success, warning or boundary feedback only when supported. Never use haptics as the sole outcome signal, repeat them continuously or trigger them on every scroll tick.

For timers and sessions, render time from a monotonic/end-time source rather than counting animation frames; restore accurately after backgrounding.

# 3D Product Scrollytelling — Exploded Assemblies & Cinematic Technical Visualization

Scroll-driven product storytelling: assembled → rotate → open → explode → focus → annotate → reassemble. This chapter owns **part-level product choreography** — exploded views, disassembly, cutaways, x-ray reveals — on the premium black-background aesthetic. It builds on [threejs-scroll-world.md](threejs-scroll-world.md) (scene architecture, R3F/vanilla wiring, lifecycle) and [motion-3d-playbook.md](motion-3d-playbook.md) (Lenis + GSAP ScrollTrigger setup); read those for the how, this for the what and the rules.

Machine-readable assets: `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` (deterministic beat maps) and `assets/scroll-scene.js` (renderer-agnostic progress engine). Reference imagery and study links: [scrollytelling-references.md](scrollytelling-references.md).

## 0. Mobile adaptation (read first on this skill)

This chapter applies to the mobile skill's **web/PWA marketing and story surfaces** — product pages, launch stories, onboarding tours rendered in a browser or webview. Adaptation deltas: pin length ≤ 350vh; DPR cap 1.5; part count ≤ 6 with merged sub-assemblies; captions render as an inline stack under the sticky scene instead of floating callouts; touch is never captured (native vertical scroll only) and horizontal gestures are reserved for the system. Fully native app shells should reuse the same beat maps through platform scroll-linked animation APIs rather than a WebView when possible.

## Contents

1. When to reach for this (and when not)
2. The primitive: scroll progress owns the scene
3. Recipe catalog
4. Beat maps
5. Rendering tiers and the never-flatten rule
6. GLB and part conventions
7. The scroll engine contract
8. UX contract (non-negotiable)
9. Performance budgets
10. Accessibility and honest duplication

## 1. When to reach for this (and when not)

Reach for it when a **physical or physically-imagined product** is the hero and its internals or construction ARE the story: hardware launches (watch, phone, GPU, drone, camera, EV component, AI chip, robot), premium DTC objects (sneaker, espresso machine), technical credibility pages ("how it's built"), and configurators that earn a narrative intro. One scrollytelling scene per page; it is the landing's "one dominant motion idea" from [landing-system.md](landing-system.md), never an addition to one.

Do **not** use it for dashboards, tools, or any surface where the person came to act rather than be told a story; where no genuine part hierarchy exists (a T-shirt is not an assembly); or where the budget only affords a flattened video — then use an ordinary media section instead of a fake-interactive one.

## 2. The primitive: scroll progress owns the scene

Normalized progress `p ∈ [0,1]` over a pinned section is the **only clock**. Every scene property — camera distance/height/orbit/fov, per-part explosion, shell opacity, clip plane, highlight, caption — is a pure function of `p`. Consequences:

- **Scrub, never play.** No timers advance the scene. Scrolling back replays backward perfectly (reversibility is free when state is a function, impossible when it's a video you fired).
- **Deterministic beats.** A recipe is a list of keyframes (`beats`) at fixed `p` values; the engine interpolates numeric fields between adjacent beats and switches discrete fields at beat boundaries.
- The scene owns real objects (Tier A) whenever possible, so `p` can drive positions, materials, lights and annotations independently — the reason this beats scrubbing a video.

## 3. Recipe catalog

Twenty deterministic recipes ship in `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json`. Pick **one primary** per scene; a second may be nested only as a sub-beat (e.g., `component-focus` inside `exploded-assembly` — the shipped `exploded-assembly` already includes two focus beats).

| Recipe | Intent | Tiers |
|---|---|---|
| `product-reveal` | Darkness → rim light → silhouette → full product | A B C |
| `exploded-assembly` | The canonical: rotate, explode, focus ×2, reassemble | A B |
| `product-disassembly` | Parts leave one by one in service order | A B |
| `internal-reveal` | Shell fades, internals stay lit | A B |
| `layer-peel` | Concentric layers lift in sequence (shoe, battery, PCB stack) | A B |
| `component-focus` | Camera dollies to one part; rest dims; spec appears | A B |
| `xray-reveal` | Materials go translucent by scroll; skeleton/frame glows | A |
| `material-transformation` | Raw material → machined → finished surface | A B C |
| `assembly-sequence` | Parts fly in and seat (reverse disassembly) | A B |
| `floating-components` | Parts drift in loose formation; labels attach | A |
| `orbital-inspection` | 360° orbit with 3–5 annotated stations | A B |
| `camera-fly-through` | Camera travels through the open product | A |
| `mechanical-operation` | One mechanism cycles as scroll advances (gears, hinge, shutter) | A B |
| `product-morph` | Model A transitions to model B (generations, sizes) | A |
| `cutaway-reveal` | Clip plane sweeps a cross-section | A |
| `particle-assembly` | Product condenses from particles, then solidifies | A |
| `technical-blueprint` | Wireframe/blueprint style resolves into rendered product | A |
| `reassembly-hero` | Exploded start; scroll assembles toward CTA | A B |
| `macro-zoom` | Extreme close-up travels the surface to a wide hero | A B C |
| `hero-to-grid` | Hero product recedes into a comparison/spec grid handoff | A B |

## 4. Beat maps

A beat map is the recipe's spine. Format (see the JSON for full schema):

```json
{ "p": 0.42, "label": "internals-emerge",
  "state": { "rotY": 0.35, "explode": 0.7, "shellFade": 0.85,
             "focus": -1, "camDist": 3.2, "camHeight": 0.4, "fov": 40 },
  "caption": "flight-controller" }
```

Worked ledger for `exploded-assembly` (the shipped default):

```
p 0.00  black; rim light only            0.52  full exploded state
  0.06  silhouette resolves              0.62  camera approaches board
  0.12  key light up, product assembled  0.70  board highlighted + spec caption
  0.20  slow quarter turn                0.78  second focus: battery + caption
  0.30  shell separates                  0.86  components return
  0.42  internals emerge                 0.95  reassembled, settle turn
                                         1.00  CTA handoff
```

Rules: beats are monotonic in `p`; first beat at 0 and last at 1; **something must visibly change within the first 0.05** (immediate feedback); captions attach to beats, and every caption's content also exists in the plain-DOM narrative (§10).

## 5. Rendering tiers and the never-flatten rule

**Tier A — real-time 3D (default).** GLB/glTF parts → Three.js or R3F; `p` drives transforms, materials, lights. Choose whenever a part hierarchy exists or can be modeled.
**Tier B — rendered frame sequence.** Blender/C4D render → WebP/AVIF frames → canvas scrub (the Apple AirPods technique). Choose for photoreal scenes too heavy for live rendering. Frames are still driven by the same beat map (`frame = round(p × (N−1))`); captions and landmarks stay real DOM.
**Tier C — video scrub.** `video.currentTime = p × duration`. Last resort only: seeking is imprecise and keyframe-dependent, reversal stutters, parts can't be addressed. Requires an all-keyframe (I-frame) encode.

**The asset rule: never flatten a usable multipart 3D product into video if the component hierarchy can be preserved.** A watch, phone, GPU, server, engine, drone, sneaker or robot with separable parts becomes an interactive scroll narrative (Tier A), not decorative footage. Downgrade tiers only for photorealism the GPU budget can't carry (→ B) or when the source simply isn't reconstructable (→ C).

## 6. GLB and part conventions

- **Hierarchy**: one root `product`; direct children are addressable parts named `part_<slug>` in disassembly order (`part_glass`, `part_screen`, `part_board`, `part_battery`, `part_shell_back`). Sub-assemblies nest one level max.
- **Pivots** sit at each part's *assembled* position; explosion is a translation from rest, so `explode = 0` is always exactly the assembled product.
- **Explosion vectors** live in a JSON sidecar (or glTF `extras`): `{ "part_glass": { "dir": [0,1,0], "dist": 1.2, "order": 1 } }` — per-part direction (unit), distance (in product-radius units), and stagger order. Configurable per component, ExplodeView-style.
- **Scale/units**: meters; product normalized so its bounding radius ≈ 1 — camera distances in recipes are multiples of it.
- **Compression**: Draco or Meshopt; textures KTX2 (fallback WebP) ≤ 2048px; PBR with one material per part so dim/highlight is a per-part `opacity`/`emissive` write, never a shared-material mutation.
- Author the black-background look in the scene (rim + key lights, dark env), not baked into textures, so packs can retint via `--ifx-grad-a/b` accent lights.

## 7. The scroll engine contract

`assets/scroll-scene.js` (`window.IFXScrollScene`) is dependency-free and renderer-agnostic — it computes progress and interpolated beat state; Three.js, canvas-sequence or video adapters consume it. GSAP ScrollTrigger can replace it 1:1 where already present (map `self.progress` to the same beat interpolation).

```js
const scene = IFXScrollScene.create({
  section: document.querySelector('#story'),   // tall pinned section
  beats: recipes['exploded-assembly'].beats,
  onUpdate(state, p, info) { /* write state.* into your renderer */ },
  onBeat(beat, dir) { /* captions, landmarks, aria-live */ },
});
```

Guarantees: passive listeners only (never preventDefault — no scroll hijacking); rAF-coalesced updates only while the section intersects; numeric fields eased between beats, discrete fields switched at beats; `prefers-reduced-motion` detected and (by default) progress quantized to beat states — stepped, still reversible; `destroy()` releases everything. Helpers: `lerp, remap, clamp, ease.*`.

## 8. UX contract (non-negotiable)

Field feedback on scroll-driven 3D sites is consistent: people abandon when scrolling feels dead and get disoriented when reversing misbehaves. Every scrollytelling scene therefore ships with:

1. **Immediate feedback** — visible change within the first 5% of the pin; never a long dead zone before the scene "starts".
2. **Reversible timeline** — scrolling up exactly rewinds; no one-way triggers, no re-fired entrance animations.
3. **Landmarks** — a progress rail with labeled beat dots that are real buttons (scroll-to on activation); current beat reflected in text.
4. **No scroll hijacking** — native scroll + `position: sticky`; wheel/touch are never captured or re-timed. (Smoothing via Lenis is acceptable; capturing is not.)
5. **Honest pin length** — 300–600vh desktop; more scroll than story is padding, less is whiplash.
6. **Reduced motion** — stepped beat states or a static poster + the full text narrative; parallax and particle drift removed.
7. **Mobile simplification** — pin ≤ 350vh, DPR ≤ 1.5, part count and lights reduced, captions become an inline stack; touch never fights vertical scroll.
8. **Escape hatch** — content after the pin is reachable by keyboard and a "skip story" link precedes the scene.

## 9. Performance budgets

Hero scene ≤ 150k triangles, ≤ 80 draw calls, textures ≤ 2048 KTX2/WebP, total 3D payload ≤ 6 MB (Tier B: frames ≤ 4 MB via AVIF/WebP ~85% quality, ≤ 160 frames, resolution-switched by viewport). Lazy-init on approach (IntersectionObserver, one viewport early); pause rendering when off-screen; cap `devicePixelRatio` at 2 (1.5 mobile); scene update ≤ 8 ms on a mid-tier phone. Preload strategy for Tier B: first + last frames immediately, the rest in idle time, decode ahead of the scrub direction.

## 10. Accessibility and honest duplication

The canvas is `aria-hidden`; the story exists in parallel as ordinary DOM: headings per act, the same captions and spec values in a plain section after the pin (the "spec sheet" duplicates every annotated number). Beat changes may announce politely (throttled) via a visually-hidden live region. Focus order ignores the scene entirely; the progress-rail buttons are the only interactive scene chrome. If WebGL is unavailable, render the poster + narrative — the page must still sell the product with zero JavaScript-driven motion.

Reference translation law applies here as everywhere: study the linked material for **beat timing, camera language, lighting-on-black, part choreography and annotation style** — never copy a specific product's model, footage, or composition.

# Platform adaptation

Select implementation from the existing project and target platform. Do not introduce cross-platform technology solely because the brief says “mobile.”

## Mobile web and PWA

- Use semantic HTML, resilient routing, responsive CSS, viewport/safe-area handling and install/offline behavior only when the product needs it.
- Test dynamic browser chrome, virtual keyboard resizing, back/forward history, standalone mode and reduced/data-saving preferences.
- Avoid imitating native controls so closely that browser behavior becomes misleading.

## iOS and iPadOS

- Follow platform navigation stacks, sheets, tab bars, safe areas, Dynamic Type, VoiceOver and system appearance.
- Preserve swipe-back only when the navigation stack supports it; never conflict with system edge gestures.
- Adapt phone compositions for split view, pointer/keyboard and larger content regions on iPad.

## Android

- Follow system Back, predictive back where supported, window insets, TalkBack, font/display scaling and Material/platform behavior already present in the app.
- Use at least 48dp touch targets and ensure edge-to-edge content remains clear of system bars.
- Support compact, medium and expanded window classes when tablets/foldables are in scope.

## React Native and Flutter

- Reuse the established navigation, state, accessibility and theming packages.
- Map semantic roles to platform primitives and verify actual native focus, text scaling, keyboard and lifecycle behavior.
- Do not claim pixel-identical parity; preserve task, hierarchy and brand while respecting platform conventions.

## Capability gate

If no simulator/device or rendered preview is available, perform code-level and unit checks, document unverified visual/device behavior and avoid device-specific quality claims.
